:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Given that $y= 3\cdot 2^{1 - x},$ find $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y = 3\cdot 2^u, \qquad u=1-x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = 3\cdot 2^u\ln(2),\qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} =-1.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =3\cdot {2}^{u}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\cdot (-1) \\  & =-3\cdot {2}^{u}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\  & =-3\cdot {2}^{1-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y={4}^{7x}$ at the point where $x=\frac{1}{7}.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={4}^{u},\,u=7x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}={4}^{u}ln⁡4,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=7.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={4}^{u}ln⁡4\cdot 7 \\  & =7ln⁡4\cdot {4}^{u} \\  & =7ln⁡4\cdot {4}^{7x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=\frac{1}{7}$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{x=1/7} & =7ln⁡(4)\cdot {4}^{7(1/7)} \\  & =7ln⁡(4)\cdot 4 \\  & =28ln⁡(4)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $x=\frac{1}{7}$ is $28ln⁡(4).$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y={4}^{2x+1}$ at the point where $x=-1.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={4}^{u},\,u=2x+1.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}={4}^{u}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4),\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={4}^{u}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)\cdot 2 \\  & =2\cdot {4}^{2x+1}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=-1$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point. 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=-1} & ={(2\cdot {4}^{2x+1}\operatorname{ln}⁡4)|}_{x=-1} \\  & =2\cdot {4}^{-1}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((4)^{1/2}) \\  & =ln\,(\,\sqrt{4}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the $y$-value of the point on the curve where $x={x}_{1}=-1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & ={({4}^{2x+1})|}_{x=-1} \\  & ={4}^{2(-1)+1} \\  & ={4}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at that point:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-\frac{1}{4} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\cdot (x+1) \\ y-\frac{1}{4} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\,x+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\,x+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
f = e^u, \qquad u=5x+4.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} = e^u,\qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} =5.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{u}\cdot 5 \\  & =5{e}^{u} \\  & =5{e}^{5x+4}.\end{aligned}

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
The chain rule can be used to differentiate exponential functions like 

$$
y = e^{3x}.
$$

First, notice that this function can be written as the composite function

$$
y = e^u, \qquad u = 3x.
$$

We can use the chain rule to compute the derivative of this composite function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}({e}^{u})\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3x) \\  & ={e}^{u}\cdot 3 \\  & =3{e}^{u}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $u=3x,$ we obtain the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{e}^{3x}\end{aligned}
$$
